tldr: Pressler argues that Java's big runtime, with speculative JIT compilation, generational moving GCs and JFR, exists to remove the overheads low-level languages accumulate in large, evolving programs, making those programs faster in practice.
summary: Ron Pressler, a former C++ developer, says that programmers without long low-level experience wrongly assume small runtimes mean fast programs. He defines a runtime as any code in the program that is not compiled from application code. He rejects the mathematical definition of language speed because it ignores what it costs to write the faster program, and the relevant question is how fast the programs we can actually afford to write are. Abstraction makes code easy to change, while optimization needs implementation details. He illustrates this with a C++ Shape class whose virtual call must be monomorphized with templates, a change that spreads through every caller. He quotes Andrew Kelley of Zig calling this a fundamental trade-off with the 'laws of physics'.

Java's answer is to compile after runtime information is known. HotSpot profiles call sites, speculatively inlines the observed implementation, and deoptimizes if the guess turns out wrong. That removes the abstraction cost which an AOT compiler can only avoid when it can prove the call target. The trade-offs are warm-up, which cached compiled code can largely remove, and a worse worst case after deoptimization, which suits Java's statistical aim of fast average performance more than low-level languages' focus on the worst case. He also argues that benchmarks are basically useless for generalizing: JITs, contention-dependent data structures, allocator state, caches and branch prediction all depend on the whole program.

On memory, freeing objects one at a time when the compiler knows they are dead is less efficient than reclaiming memory in bulk, as moving collectors and arenas do. Generational moving GCs effectively use spare RAM to save CPU, and the headroom they need scales with allocation rate, not live data. In a colleague's experiment, Caffeine on ZGC used 5% more RAM than Rust's Moka but had lower latencies at every percentile and twice the throughput. Java spent 20% of CPU on memory management, while Rust spent 40% just deciding when to free. Low-level languages cannot adopt moving GCs because they need stable pointers for FFI. Java's real remaining handicap is array memory layout, which Project Valhalla addresses through semantic declarations rather than manual control.

He closes with JFR, which offers deep telemetry at about 1–2% overhead, more than eBPF can see in a C++ program. He suggests that an AI capable of re-optimizing large programs might skip compilers altogether. His tips for language designers: know types at runtime, keep a strict FFI boundary, disallow pointers into the stack, and build in low-overhead telemetry. His advice to Java developers is to write natural code and distrust JVM folklore. Object pooling, for instance, now hurts, because mutating old-generation objects costs more than allocating new ones.
keyPoints: 'Language X is faster' should mean faster for the programs we can actually afford to write, not programs that could exist in principle.
Abstraction cost (e.g. C++ virtual calls) forces viral specialization in low-level languages; HotSpot removes it by profiling, speculative inlining and deoptimization.
Microbenchmarks rarely generalize because JIT decisions, allocator fast/slow paths, contention, caches and branch prediction depend on the whole program.
Generational moving collectors trade RAM for CPU; required headroom depends on allocation rate, not heap size of live data.
Caffeine on ZGC vs Rust's Moka: about 5% more RAM, better latency at all percentiles, roughly 2x throughput; 20% vs 40%+ CPU on memory management.
Moving GCs and deoptimizing JITs need an FFI boundary, which is why low-level languages, built for direct hardware access, cannot use them.
Java's remaining structural disadvantage is arrays of references; Valhalla flattens values based on declared intent (no identity, non-null).
JFR provides production profiling at roughly 1–2% overhead; avoid object pooling purely to save allocations, as old-gen mutation is costlier.
takeaways: Profile your actual application, in development and in production with JFR, instead of trusting microbenchmarks.
Write natural, abstract Java code and let the JIT specialize it; revisit any hand-optimizations when you upgrade the JDK.
Stop pooling plain objects to avoid allocation; allocate new objects and give the GC enough heap.
Treat GC CPU usage seen in telemetry in context: manual memory management also costs CPU, it is just less visible.

quotes.text: Benchmarks are basically useless. It's not that the measurements are wrong, but that they're only true if your entire program is the benchmark.
Generational moving collectors effectively turn RAM chips into hardware accelerators.
If you need a new object, just create a new one. Don't reuse an existing one.

watchIf: You have heard that Java is slow because of its JIT and GC, or you hand-optimize Java on old folklore, and want the reasoning from the Java platform group behind why the runtime is designed this way.
